newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian activists postpone police abuse forum.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian activists postpone police abuse forum.

text.p: Faced with threats of arrest, a group of Malaysian human rights activists said on Saturday it had decided to postpone indefinitely a public forum on alleged police abuses.

Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said this week that the non-governmental organisations (NGOs) that planned to hold the "Tribunal Rakyat" (People's Tribunal) forum would be arrested if they held the public meeting without a police permit.
All public gatherings in Malaysia require a permit. Mahathir said the authorities might be forced to use the Internal Security Act (ISA), which allows for detention of up to two years without trial.
"If the situation becomes bad, we may have to use the ISA," Mahathir was quoted by a newspaper on Thursday as saying. "The ISA is designed for people who are irresponsible and traitorous."

In a statement faxed to the media on Saturday, the NGOs said: "In view of the tense environment created by repeated threats to use the ISA and various other irresponsible statements in the media attacking the integrity of the organisers, we are postponing the Tribunal indefinitely.

"In the meantime, we will continue to raise cases of abuses of police powers through whatever means available to us. The organisers will be waiting for the police to decide on a time and venue for such a dialogue."
The statement carried the names of nine NGOs.
The forum was originally planned for December 15 but was rescheduled to January when Deputy Home Minister Megat Junid raised the issue about a police permit.
Organisers of the forum had said the discussion would be "based on actual experiences and outcome of abuse of police powers".
Malaysian police have challenged the accusations of abuse, saying they have always treated allegations of misconduct by their members with "care and sensitivity".

The proposed forum follows an aborted meeting on East Timor in November. After proceeding with the conference despite government warnings, the Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor II (APCET II) was broken up by pro-government youths.
Malaysia had objected to APCET II in deference to neighbour Indonesia, which invaded the former Portugese colony in 1975 and rules it in defiance of the United Nations.
The Tribunal Rakyat said its forum is not connected to APCET II and was organised independently of that meeting.
